newsitem.title: FRANCE: French calls for looser approach to euro.
newsitem.headline: French calls for looser approach to euro.

text.p: The European Union must not enforce niggling conditions in deciding which countries qualify for a single European currency and should allow as many as possible to join, French National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin said.

Seguin, a leading contender to become prime minister if the centre-right wins the second round of a parliamentary election on Sunday, also said French voters were still awaiting an answer from President Jacques Chirac to the economic problems he set out to solve in 1995.
"We have not yet had this answer," Seguin said in an interview with the weekly l'Express due to appear on Wednesday.

French voters dealt Chirac a sharp rebuff in the first-round vote two days ago, giving the left a solid lead and forcing Prime Minister Alain Juppe to promise he would step down after this weekend's run-off regardless of the result.

Seguin said he hoped an economic straitjacket imposed on France in pursuit of the single European currency could be eased once the launch of the euro removed the need to reassure the German public about abandoning the deutschemark.
"We are in a straitjacket. I dare hope that once the euro is launched and we no longer need to convince German public opinion, we will loosen it," he said.

Many European countries are struggling to cut their public deficits to three percent of gross domestic product as the Maastricht Treaty on monetary union requires. This effort has hit economic growth and hurt jobs creation.
"There should not be a petty bookkeeper's approach to the entry conditions for the euro," Seguin said. "The maximum number of countries must participate."
Seguin said the fight against inflation must not be the only preoccupation. Employment was "the priority of priorities".
"A target of three percent of deficits in a period of expansion is not virtuous. In a period of austerity it is masochism," he added.
Seguin, who campaigned against Maastricht in a 1992 referendum, added that Paris must honour the treaty since "France's signature is committed....That signature must be honoured."
He said the lead taken by the combined left in the first round of voting was "a message addressed to the president".

French people had great hopes in 1995, the year of the presidential election, that the political establishment would provide an answer to their economic problems which offered a "third way" combining liberalism with the needs of society.
"The policies undertaken since 1995 by Jacques Chirac must be continued in the direction he indicated in the presidential campaign," Seguin said.
